subjects.name: Integrated Science
mcq: Which rule should a learner follow before using laboratory apparatus?
Read the instructions and obtain permission
Reading instructions and following the teacher's directions prevents accidents.
What should a learner do after a chemical splashes into the eyes?
Rinse immediately with plenty of clean running water and report
Cover both eyes and continue working
Immediate flushing and reporting are essential first-aid steps.
Which apparatus is designed to measure liquid volume accurately?
A measuring cylinder has graduations for measuring liquid volume.
Which instrument is commonly used to heat substances in a school laboratory?
A Bunsen burner provides a flame for heating.
Which part of a Bunsen burner regulates the amount of air entering?
Turning the collar opens or closes the air hole.
What is the function of the air hole in a Bunsen burner?
To admit air for mixing with gas
To connect the burner to a tap
Air mixes with the gas and affects combustion and flame characteristics.
Which part of a Bunsen burner connects it to the gas supply?
The gas hose carries gas from the supply to the burner.
Why should the base of a Bunsen burner be broad and stable?
To prevent the burner from toppling
A stable base reduces the risk of the burner falling.
Which gas forms the largest proportion of air?
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air.
Which gas is needed for ordinary combustion?
Which gas do green plants use during photosynthesis?
Plants take in carbon dioxide to make food during photosynthesis.
Which gas is released by green plants during photosynthesis?
Oxygen is released as a product of photosynthesis.
Which method can reduce friction between moving machine parts?
Lubricants form a layer that reduces direct contact between surfaces.
Which surface is likely to produce the greatest friction when pushed against another?
Rough surfaces interlock more than smooth surfaces.
Why are treads made on the soles of shoes?
Treads improve friction between shoes and the ground.
A force that opposes relative motion between surfaces
A force that always pulls objects upwards
Friction acts against sliding or attempted sliding between surfaces.
Which blood group is commonly called the universal red-cell donor group?
O negative red cells lack A, B and Rh(D) antigens; transfusion still requires professional compatibility checks.
Which blood group has both A and B antigens on red blood cells?
AB red blood cells carry both A and B antigens.
The skull encloses and protects the brain.
Which bone is found in the upper arm?
The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm.
Which bone is found in the thigh?
The femur is the thigh bone and is the longest bone in the human body.
Which bone is located in the lower leg and is commonly called the shin bone?
The tibia is the larger bone in the lower leg.
Which bone is found in the forearm on the thumb side?
The radius is one of the two forearm bones and lies on the thumb side in anatomical position.
What is the main function of the rib cage?
To protect the heart and lungs
The ribs form a protective cage around organs in the chest.
Which part of the skeleton supports the trunk and attaches the lower limbs?
The pelvis supports the trunk and forms the connection to the lower limbs.
Which organ pumps blood around the body?
The heart is a muscular pump that circulates blood.
Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
What is the function of the lungs in the circulatory and respiratory systems?
Gas exchange occurs between air in the lungs and blood.
Which instrument is used to view very small objects that cannot be seen clearly with the naked eye?
How should a learner carry a light microscope?
By holding the arm and supporting the base
By swinging it by the cord
Holding the arm and supporting the base helps prevent dropping and damage.
Which apparatus is used to transfer small quantities of liquid drop by drop?
A dropper delivers liquid in small drops.
Which item is suitable for a basic first-aid kit?
Sterile gauze can cover wounds and help control bleeding.
What is the first action when a learner notices a minor bleeding wound?
Apply clean pressure using sterile dressing
Leave it uncovered in dirty surroundings
Clean direct pressure helps control bleeding; serious wounds need urgent adult/medical help.
A substance has a mass of 200 g and a volume of 50 cm³. What is its density?
A block has a mass of 90 g and a volume of 30 cm³. Calculate its density.
A liquid is measured in a measuring cylinder. At which part of the meniscus should water be read?
Bottom of the meniscus at eye level
Top of the meniscus from above
For water and most clear liquids, read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Why should the eye be level with the meniscus when taking a reading?
Viewing at eye level reduces reading errors caused by parallax.
Which tool is most suitable for measuring the mass of a small solid object?
Which indicator can be used to help identify whether a solution is acidic or basic?
Litmus changes colour in acidic and alkaline solutions.
What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acidic solution?
Acids turn blue litmus paper red.
Which practice is safest when heating a test tube?
Point its open end away from people
The open end should point away from everyone because hot liquid or vapour may spurt.
Which part of a microscope is looked through when viewing a specimen?
The eyepiece is the lens through which the learner looks.
Which microscope part holds the slide in position?
Stage clips keep the slide steady on the stage.
Which microscope control is used for rough focusing at low power?
The coarse adjustment knob makes large focusing movements, usually at low power.
Which apparatus is used to measure temperature?
Which apparatus is used to support a beaker during heating?
A tripod stand supports apparatus above a flame.
What is the role of wire gauze during heating?
Spread heat and support a container
Wire gauze supports glassware and helps distribute heat.
Which action is unsafe when working with a Bunsen burner?
A lit burner should never be left unattended.
What should be done before lighting a Bunsen burner?
Check the hose and follow the teacher's lighting procedure
Open the gas fully and walk away
Touch the barrel to test it
The equipment should be checked and lit only under supervision.
Why is a blue Bunsen burner flame generally hotter than a yellow luminous flame?
More air mixes with the gas, allowing more complete combustion
Greater air supply supports more complete combustion and a hotter flame.
Which gas is essential for aerobic respiration?
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from food.
Which gas is present in air in the greatest amount after nitrogen?
Oxygen makes up about 21% of dry air.
Which statement about carbon dioxide in air is correct?
It is present in a small proportion and used in photosynthesis
It is the main gas used in breathing
It is absent from the atmosphere
Carbon dioxide is a trace gas used by plants in photosynthesis.
Which gas is commonly used in some fire extinguishers because it does not support combustion?
Carbon dioxide can displace oxygen around a fire and is used in suitable extinguishers.
Which of these is an example of friction being harmful?
A car stopping when brakes are applied
Friction can cause wear and unwanted heating in machine parts.
Which change is most likely to increase friction between two surfaces?
Why do vehicle tyres have grooves?
To improve grip and help channel water away
Grooves improve traction, especially on wet roads.
Which statement about friction is correct?
It always makes objects move faster
It has no effect on motion
Friction converts some mechanical energy into heat.
Which blood group has neither A nor B antigen on red blood cells?
Group O red cells lack A and B antigens.
Which blood group has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma in the basic ABO system?
Group O plasma normally contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
Which blood group has A antigen and anti-B antibodies in the basic ABO system?
Group A red cells carry A antigen; plasma normally has anti-B antibodies.
Which bone forms the shoulder-to-elbow part of the arm?
The humerus extends from the shoulder to the elbow.
Which pair consists of bones in the forearm?
The radius and ulna are the two forearm bones.
Which bone protects the spinal cord?
The vertebrae surround and protect the spinal cord.
Which part of the skeleton protects the lungs?
The rib cage surrounds the chest and protects the lungs.
Which organ receives oxygen-poor blood from the body before it is sent to the lungs?
The right side of the heart receives blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs.
Which side of the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body?
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and body.
What is the main function of capillaries?
Allow exchange of substances between blood and tissues
Pump blood out of the heart
Their thin walls allow exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes.
Which first-aid action is appropriate for a small superficial burn?
Cool it under cool running water and report it
Cool running water helps limit tissue damage; report the injury and seek help.
Why should disposable gloves be used when giving first aid to a bleeding person?
To reduce contact with blood and infection risk
To make the wound bleed faster
To stop the need for medical help
Gloves provide a barrier against blood-borne infection.
Which item is best for securing a wound dressing?
A bandage can hold a dressing in place.
A solid has a mass of 72 g and a volume of 9 cm³. What is its density?
A liquid has a density of 2 g/cm³ and a volume of 15 cm³. What is its mass?
A substance has a mass of 48 g and density of 6 g/cm³. What is its volume?
Which unit is appropriate for density of a small solid measured in grams and cubic centimetres?
Density is mass divided by volume, so g/cm³ is appropriate.
If an object is fully immersed in water, the rise in water level represents the object's what?
The displaced water volume equals the volume of the immersed object.
Which reading is correct for a clear water meniscus?
The highest point of the curve
Read the bottom of the concave meniscus at eye level.
What does red litmus paper do in an alkaline solution?
Alkalis turn red litmus paper blue.
Which of the following is a safe way to smell a substance when instructed to do so?
Waft vapour gently towards the nose
Put the nose directly over the container
Shake the container near the face
Wafting reduces direct exposure to concentrated vapours.
Which precaution should be taken when diluting or mixing laboratory solutions under teacher instruction?
Add substances carefully and follow the teacher's method
Careful handling and following instructions reduce splashes and exposure.
structured: State four laboratory safety rules that learners should observe during practical lessons.

Award 1 mark each for any four: follow teacher instructions; do not taste chemicals; do not run; wear protective gear where required; report spills/injuries; handle glassware carefully; keep the work area tidy.
Explain the correct response when a chemical accidentally splashes onto a learner's skin.

Award up to 3 marks: rinse affected skin immediately with plenty of clean running water; remove contaminated clothing/jewellery while rinsing if safe; inform the teacher and seek appropriate medical attention.
Name two laboratory heating instruments and state one use of each.
Award 1 mark for each correct instrument and use: Bunsen burner—heating; spirit burner—heating; hot plate—heating substances/solutions.
Describe two ways of reducing friction between moving machine parts and explain how each works.
Award 2 marks each: lubrication separates surfaces; use rollers/ball bearings changes sliding friction to rolling friction; polishing smooths surfaces. Explanation required.
Give two situations in daily life where friction is useful and explain its importance.
Award 1 mark for each valid situation and 1 for explanation: walking—grip; vehicle brakes—slows/stops wheels; writing—pencil/pen grips paper; tyre treads—traction.
State four components of air and give an approximate proportion or role for each.
Award 1 mark each: nitrogen about 78%; oxygen about 21%; argon and other noble gases about 0.9%; carbon dioxide about 0.04% (values may be approximate).
Explain two uses of oxygen and two uses of carbon dioxide.

Award 1 mark each: oxygen supports respiration; oxygen supports combustion/medical oxygen; carbon dioxide used by plants in photosynthesis; carbon dioxide used in fire extinguishers or carbonated drinks.
Draw and label a Bunsen burner, showing the base, gas inlet, gas hose, collar, air hole and barrel.
Award marks for a recognisable outline (1) and correct labels (up to 5).
Describe the function of the collar, air hole, base, gas hose and gas inlet of a Bunsen burner.
Award 1 mark each: collar opens/closes air hole; air hole admits air; base supports burner; gas hose conveys gas; gas inlet admits gas into burner.
Distinguish between a luminous flame and a non-luminous flame produced by a Bunsen burner.
Award 1 mark each for colour/appearance, air supply, temperature/soot: luminous is yellow, less air, cooler/sooty; non-luminous is blue, more air, hotter/cleaner.
Name four blood groups in the ABO system and state the antigens found on their red blood cells.
Award 1 mark each: A—A antigen; B—B antigen; AB—A and B antigens; O—neither A nor B antigen.
State four functions of the human skeleton.
Award 1 mark each: support; protection of internal organs; movement with muscles; blood-cell production in bone marrow; mineral storage.
Identify the bones that form the skull, upper arm, thigh, lower leg and forearm.
Award 1 mark each: skull; humerus; femur; tibia; radius (ulna may also be named for the forearm).
Explain how the rib cage protects internal organs.
Award up to 3 marks: ribs form a cage around the chest; protect the heart and lungs; the cage moves during breathing while providing protection.
Describe the pathway of blood through the heart and lungs in a simplified sequence.
Award up to 4 marks: body to right side of heart; right side pumps blood to lungs; lungs oxygenate blood; blood returns to left side; left side pumps blood to the body.
State three ways of handling and caring for a light microscope.
Award 1 mark each: carry with two hands (arm and base); place on a stable bench; clean lenses with lens tissue; start with low-power objective; store covered after use.
Name four apparatus commonly found in a Grade 7 laboratory and state one use of each.

Award 1 mark for each correct apparatus-use pair, e.g. measuring cylinder—volume; beaker—holding/mixing; thermometer—temperature; balance—mass; dropper—small liquid quantities; test tube—small reactions.
List four items that may be found in a first-aid kit and state one use of each.

Award 1 mark per correct item-use pair: sterile gauze/dressing—cover wound; bandage—secure dressing; adhesive plasters—small cuts; antiseptic wipes—clean around minor wounds; gloves—barrier protection.
A learner has a cut that is bleeding. Describe the steps an adult should take to give basic first aid.

Award up to 4 marks: ensure scene safety and use gloves/barrier; apply firm direct pressure with clean dressing; seek adult/medical assistance for severe or persistent bleeding; do not remove soaked dressing—add another layer; reassure learner.
Define density and write the formula used to calculate it.
Award 1 mark for mass per unit volume; 1 mark for density = mass ÷ volume (D = m/V).
A metal block has a mass of 360 g and a volume of 45 cm³. Calculate its density, showing your working.
Award 1 mark for formula; 1 for substitution; 1 for correct answer 8 g/cm³.
A stone has a mass of 150 g. Its volume is 60 cm³. Calculate its density and include the correct unit.
Award 1 mark for formula/substitution; 1 for calculation; 1 for 2.5 g/cm³.
Explain how the volume of an irregular solid can be found using water displacement.
Award up to 4 marks: record initial water volume; lower object fully without splashing; record final volume; subtract initial from final; difference is object volume.
Describe how to read the volume of water in a measuring cylinder accurately.
Award up to 3 marks: place cylinder upright on level bench; allow water to settle; position eye level with meniscus; read bottom of meniscus for water.
What is a meniscus? Explain why it forms in a measuring cylinder.
Award 2 marks: curved upper surface of a liquid; caused by interaction/adhesion between liquid and container and cohesion within the liquid.
A learner reads water in a measuring cylinder from above the meniscus. Name the error and explain how it can be avoided.
Award 2 marks: parallax error; place eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
Distinguish between an acid and a base using litmus paper.
Award 2 marks: acid turns blue litmus red; base/alkali turns red litmus blue (for soluble bases).
State two precautions when using a microscope to observe a slide.
Award 2 marks: begin with low power; use coarse adjustment only on low power; avoid allowing objective lens to hit slide; use fine adjustment for sharp focus; handle slide carefully.
Explain why a learner should not taste or directly smell laboratory chemicals.
Award 2 marks: substances may be poisonous/corrosive/irritating; vapours may harm the respiratory system; unknown substances must not be tested by tasting or direct sniffing.
A learner mixes two unknown substances and notices heat and gas. State three actions the learner should take.
Award 1 mark each: stop mixing; move away if unsafe and avoid inhaling fumes; alert teacher immediately; do not touch/taste mixture; follow teacher's emergency instructions.
Explain the difference between mass and volume, giving the unit commonly used for each in the laboratory.
Mass is the amount of matter (g or kg); volume is the space occupied (cm³ or mL). Award 1 mark for each correct definition and 1 for each suitable unit.
A learner measures 25 mL of water. Convert this volume into cubic centimetres.
Award 1 mark for recognising 1 mL = 1 cm³ and 1 mark for 25 cm³.
A stone is placed in a measuring cylinder. Water rises from 40 cm³ to 57 cm³. Determine the volume of the stone and show the calculation.
Award 1 mark for subtraction; 1 mark for 57 − 40; 1 mark for 17 cm³.
Describe two sources of error when measuring liquid volume and how to reduce each error.
Award 1 mark per error and 1 per remedy: parallax—read at eye level; tilted cylinder—stand upright; unsettled liquid—allow it to settle; wrong meniscus point—read bottom for water.
State the relationship between density, mass and volume, and rearrange the formula to make mass the subject.
Award 1 mark for D=m/V; 1 mark for m=D×V.
A sample has density 5 g/cm³ and volume 12 cm³. Calculate its mass.
Award 1 mark for formula; 1 for substitution; 1 for 60 g.
A metal has mass 96 g and density 8 g/cm³. Calculate its volume.
Award 1 mark for formula; 1 for substitution; 1 for 12 cm³.
Explain why equal volumes of two different substances may have different masses.
Award up to 2 marks: substances have different densities; at equal volume, the substance with greater density has greater mass.
Describe the difference between arteries and veins.
Award up to 3 marks: arteries carry blood away from heart; veins carry blood towards heart; arteries generally have thicker elastic walls while veins have valves in many regions.
State the roles of the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.
Award 1 mark each: right atrium receives body blood; right ventricle pumps to lungs; left atrium receives lung blood; left ventricle pumps to body.
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
Award up to 2 marks: it pumps blood around the whole body; it must generate higher pressure than the right ventricle, which pumps to the nearby lungs.
Give three ways in which the skeleton helps the human body to move.
Award 1 mark each: bones provide attachment for muscles; joints allow movement; muscles pull on bones acting as levers.
Compare the functions of the skull and the rib cage.
Award 2 marks: skull protects brain; rib cage protects heart and lungs.
Describe the location of the femur, tibia, radius and humerus in the human body.
Award 1 mark each: femur—thigh; tibia—lower leg; radius—forearm; humerus—upper arm.
Explain why a microscope should be placed on a firm, level bench.
Award up to 2 marks: prevents it from falling; provides stable viewing and focusing.
Outline the correct sequence for focusing a prepared slide using a light microscope.
Award up to 4 marks: place slide on stage and secure; select low-power objective; look through eyepiece and use coarse focus carefully; use fine focus for a clear image; adjust light as needed.
State three ways to prevent accidents when using heating equipment.
Award 1 mark each: tie back long hair; keep flammables away; use tongs/heatproof mats; never leave flame unattended; turn off gas after use.
Explain why a learner should allow heated glassware to cool before handling it.
Award up to 2 marks: hot glass may cause burns; hot glass can look similar to cool glass, so use tongs or heatproof protection.
Describe how friction helps a cyclist to control a bicycle.
Award up to 3 marks: tyre-road friction provides grip; brake-pad friction slows wheel rotation; hand grip prevents slipping on handlebars.
State two disadvantages of excessive friction in machines and one way to reduce each disadvantage.
Award 1 mark each for wear and energy loss/heat; 1 mark each for lubrication, bearings or smoother surfaces.
Explain why friction is necessary for a person to walk without slipping.
Award up to 2 marks: shoe pushes backward against ground; friction from ground acts forward and provides grip for walking.
State the approximate percentages of nitrogen and oxygen in dry air and explain why air is described as a mixture.
Award 2 marks for nitrogen about 78% and oxygen about 21%; 1 mark because gases are physically mixed, not chemically combined, and proportions can vary slightly.
Describe an investigation to show that air contains oxygen, identifying one observation and a safety precaution.
Award up to 3 marks: describe a suitable teacher-supervised demonstration; observation showing oxygen supports combustion; include safe handling of flame/hot apparatus and adult supervision.
Give two reasons why oxygen is important to living things and one reason why carbon dioxide is important to plants.
Award 1 mark each: oxygen used in aerobic respiration; supports energy release; carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis.
Explain why carbon dioxide can help put out some fires.
Award up to 2 marks: it does not support combustion; it can form a layer that reduces oxygen reaching the fire. Mention suitable extinguisher use only.
State four functions of a first-aid kit in a school setting.
Award 1 mark each: provide immediate basic care; protect wounds; control minor bleeding; reduce contamination; support safe response while help is obtained.
Describe the precautions to take before helping a learner who has collapsed in the laboratory.
Award up to 3 marks: check scene safety; call teacher/first aider; do not crowd or move learner unnecessarily; check responsiveness/breathing only if trained; seek emergency help.
Explain why a learner should report every laboratory injury, even if it appears minor.
Award up to 2 marks: injuries may worsen or become infected; teacher can provide correct first aid and record/monitor incident.
Distinguish between an acid and an alkali using their effect on litmus and give one example of each.
Award 1 mark each for litmus effect and 1 each for examples: acid turns blue litmus red (e.g. vinegar/lemon juice); alkali turns red litmus blue (e.g. soap solution/limewater).
A learner obtains a density of 0.8 g/cm³ for a sample. Explain what this value means.
Award up to 2 marks: each cubic centimetre of the sample has a mass of 0.8 g.
Explain why the same mass of two materials can occupy different volumes.
Award up to 2 marks: materials may have different densities; lower-density material occupies a larger volume for the same mass.
A learner records a mass of 125 g and a volume of 25 cm³. Calculate density and state what the answer tells you.
Award 1 mark for D=m/V; 1 for 125÷25; 1 for 5 g/cm³; 1 for interpretation that each cm³ has mass 5 g.
State three observations that may indicate that a chemical reaction has occurred during a supervised experiment.
Award 1 mark each: colour change; gas/bubbles produced; temperature change; precipitate formed; light or new odour produced (only if safely observed).
Give two reasons why laboratory chemicals should be labelled clearly.
Award 1 mark each: identify contents; communicate hazards/precautions; prevent accidental misuse or mixing.
Describe how to respond if a glass beaker breaks during a practical lesson.
Award up to 3 marks: stop work and alert teacher; keep others away; do not pick shards with bare hands; teacher/appropriate tool clears glass into designated container.
State three differences between a measuring cylinder and a beaker.
Award 1 mark each: measuring cylinder is graduated for volume measurement; generally narrower/taller; beaker is mainly for holding/mixing/heating and gives less precise volume readings.
Explain why a measuring cylinder should be placed on a flat surface before reading a liquid volume.
Award up to 2 marks: keeps cylinder upright; helps obtain an accurate meniscus reading and avoids spillage.
Name two ways the body is protected by bones and give an example for each.
Award 1 mark per valid pair: skull protects brain; ribs protect heart/lungs; vertebrae protect spinal cord.
Describe the role of valves in the heart.
Award up to 2 marks: prevent backflow of blood; ensure blood flows in one direction through the heart.
Explain why blood must pass through the lungs before being pumped to the rest of the body.
Award up to 2 marks: blood takes in oxygen; releases carbon dioxide; oxygenated blood supplies body cells for respiration.
State two ways a learner can prevent infection when giving basic first aid.
Award 1 mark each: use disposable gloves/barrier; wash hands; use sterile/clean dressing; dispose of contaminated materials safely.
A learner measures 18 cm³ of water and adds an object. The level rises to 26 cm³. Find the object's volume and explain the method.
Award 1 mark for final minus initial; 1 for 26−18; 1 for 8 cm³; 1 for displacement explanation.
Explain why a learner should not use the coarse adjustment knob when the high-power objective is close to a slide.
Award up to 2 marks: large movement may drive objective into slide; can break slide or damage lens; use fine adjustment carefully.
Describe two differences between the luminous and non-luminous Bunsen burner flames and state which is preferred for strong heating.
Award 1 mark each for colour/air/temperature and 1 for identifying non-luminous blue flame as hotter and preferred for strong heating.
State the function of the gas inlet and the gas hose in a Bunsen burner.
Award 1 mark each: hose conveys gas from supply; gas inlet admits gas into burner.
List four pieces of information that should appear on a laboratory chemical label.
Award 1 mark each: chemical name; concentration where applicable; hazard warning/symbol; relevant handling/storage instruction; date/preparer where required.
State three actions to take before leaving the laboratory at the end of a practical lesson.
Award 1 mark each: turn off gas/water/electricity as instructed; clean work area; return apparatus; wash hands; report breakages/spills.
Explain why learners should wash their hands after a laboratory practical.
Award up to 2 marks: removes chemical/biological residues; prevents accidental ingestion or transfer of contaminants.
Name two parts of the Bunsen burner flame and describe their appearance.
Award 1 mark each for correct description: inner blue cone and outer pale-blue zone in a non-luminous flame; descriptions must be clear.
Describe how closing the air hole affects a Bunsen burner flame.
Award up to 2 marks: less air mixes with gas; flame becomes yellow/luminous and cooler, with incomplete combustion/soot.
State three precautions when using a thermometer in the laboratory.
Award 1 mark each: handle gently; keep bulb from striking container; read at eye level; do not use as a stirring rod; use suitable range.
Explain why a thermometer should not be used to stir a solution.
Award up to 2 marks: it may break; broken glass/thermometer contents may cause injury or contamination.
Describe the difference between a physical change and a chemical change, giving one example of each.
Award 1 mark for each distinction/example: physical change forms no new substance (melting ice); chemical change forms new substance(s) (rusting/combustion).
Give two examples of laboratory apparatus made of glass and state one reason glass is useful for laboratory equipment.
Award 1 mark each for apparatus: beaker, test tube, measuring cylinder, flask; 1 mark for transparency/chemical resistance/heat resistance where suitable.
State two functions of the stage and the stage clips of a light microscope.
Award 1 mark each: stage supports slide; stage clips hold slide in place.
Explain why the objective lens should not touch the microscope slide.
Award up to 2 marks: may break slide; may scratch/damage lens or specimen.
Name the two main adjustment knobs on a standard school light microscope and state their functions.
Award 1 mark each: coarse adjustment for rough focus; fine adjustment for sharper focus.
Describe the difference between mass and weight.
Award up to 2 marks: mass is amount of matter measured in grams/kilograms; weight is gravitational force measured in newtons.
A learner's object has a mass of 0.5 kg. Convert this mass into grams.
Award 1 mark for conversion factor 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 mark for 500 g.
A sample has a volume of 4 cm³ and a density of 7 g/cm³. Calculate its mass.
Award 1 mark for m = density × volume; 1 for 7 × 4; 1 for 28 g.
A sample has mass 64 g and density 8 g/cm³. Calculate its volume.
Award 1 mark for V=m/D; 1 for 64÷8; 1 for 8 cm³.
Explain why density can help distinguish between two materials of equal volume.
Award up to 2 marks: density compares mass per unit volume; for equal volumes, the denser material has greater mass.
State two precautions when using a measuring cylinder to measure a liquid.
Award 1 mark each: place upright on level bench; read at eye level; allow liquid to settle; use correct meniscus point.
Describe how to estimate the volume of a regularly shaped rectangular block using measurements.
Award up to 3 marks: measure length, width and height; multiply length × width × height; use cubic units.
A rectangular block measures 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Calculate its volume.
Award 1 mark for formula; 1 for substitution; 1 for 30 cm³.
State three functions of blood in the human body.
Award 1 mark each: transport oxygen/nutrients; carry wastes; defend against infection; help regulate temperature; clot to reduce blood loss.
Explain the role of red blood cells in the body.
Award up to 2 marks: contain haemoglobin; transport oxygen from lungs to body tissues.
State the function of white blood cells.
Award up to 2 marks: defend the body against pathogens/infection; destroy pathogens or produce antibodies.
Describe the role of platelets in blood.
Award up to 2 marks: help blood clot; reduce blood loss when a blood vessel is damaged.
Explain why the heart is described as a double pump.
Award up to 2 marks: right side pumps blood to lungs; left side pumps blood to the rest of the body.
State the names of the four chambers of the human heart.
Award 1 mark each: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Describe one difference between the function of the atria and the ventricles.
Award up to 2 marks: atria receive blood into the heart; ventricles pump blood out of the heart.
Give three ways of keeping the skeletal system healthy.
Award 1 mark each: balanced diet with calcium/vitamin D; safe physical activity; good posture; prevent injuries; adequate sunlight for vitamin D.
Explain how muscles and bones work together to produce movement at a joint.
Award up to 3 marks: muscles attach to bones by tendons; muscles contract and relax; pull bones across a joint to cause movement.
State two ways of preventing slips and falls in a science laboratory.
Award 1 mark each: clean spills promptly with teacher guidance; keep walkways clear; wear suitable footwear; do not run.
Explain why eating or drinking in a laboratory is prohibited.
Award up to 2 marks: food/drink may be contaminated; chemicals may be accidentally swallowed; contamination can affect experiments.
Name three common causes of fire in a computer or science laboratory and state one prevention measure for each.
Award 1 mark per cause-prevention pair: overloaded sockets—avoid overloading; faulty wiring—inspection/repair; unattended flame—switch off/monitor; flammable materials—store safely.
Describe the safe way to dispose of broken glass in a laboratory.
Award up to 2 marks: do not touch with bare hands; alert teacher; use brush/pan or proper tool; place in designated broken-glass container.
State two reasons for keeping the laboratory well ventilated.
Award 1 mark each: remove fumes; provide fresh air; reduce heat/build-up of vapours.
Explain why a learner should never point a heated test tube towards another person.
Award up to 2 marks: hot liquid or vapour may spurt; can cause burns or eye injury.
Give two examples of situations in which friction is useful and two in which it is undesirable.
Award 1 mark each: useful—walking/braking/gripping; undesirable—machine wear/heat/energy loss.
Describe one method of reducing friction in each of the following: a door hinge and a moving bicycle wheel.
Award 1 mark each: lubricate hinge; use lubricated bearings/ball bearings in wheel hub.
Explain why friction between a vehicle's tyres and the road is important during braking.
Award up to 2 marks: friction provides grip; enables braking force to slow/stop the vehicle; wet/loose surfaces reduce grip.
State two differences between oxygen and nitrogen in relation to living things and combustion.
Award 1 mark each: oxygen supports respiration and combustion; nitrogen does not support combustion and is used by organisms after fixation/for protein formation indirectly.
Describe one classroom demonstration that shows that oxygen supports burning. Include a safety measure.
Award up to 3 marks: teacher-supervised candle/combustion demonstration in oxygen; observation flame burns more vigorously; use eye protection/keep oxygen source and flame controlled.
Explain why oxygen in the air is important even though it forms only about one-fifth of air.
Award up to 2 marks: needed for aerobic respiration in many organisms; supports combustion.
State three ways to reduce the risk of chemical exposure during practical work.
Award 1 mark each: wear appropriate protective equipment; use small quantities; avoid touching/tasting; follow instructions; wash hands; keep containers labelled.
Describe the procedure for reporting and recording an accident in the laboratory.

Award up to 3 marks: stop work and alert teacher immediately; give accurate details of what happened/injury/substance; follow first-aid/emergency directions and ensure incident is recorded by responsible staff.
Explain why a first-aid kit should be accessible but its contents should be used responsibly.
Award up to 2 marks: quick access supports prompt response; only trained/authorised persons should use items appropriately and replenish/report use.
State two limitations of using only visual observation to identify an unknown laboratory substance.
Award 1 mark each: different substances may look alike; appearance alone cannot safely establish identity/properties; testing requires approved supervised methods.
Describe how you would compare the densities of two regular solid blocks using a balance and ruler.
Award up to 4 marks: measure mass of each; measure dimensions; calculate volume; calculate density for each; compare values.

subjects.name: IRE
mcq: Which is used for Wudhu when available and suitable?
Wudhu is performed using pure water.
Tayammum is dry ablution using clean earth.
Istinjaa is cleansing after answering the call of nature.
The person who calls the Adhan is the:
Announce that the prayer is about to begin
Iqaamah signals the immediate commencement of congregational prayer.
structured: Define Swalah.
The prescribed acts of worship/prayer performed by Muslims at appointed times with specified conditions. (2)
State three essential conditions of Swalah.
Purity, covering the awrah, facing the Qibla where required, entry of prayer time, intention. Any three.
Define Twahara and Najaasat.
Twahara is ritual purity/cleanliness (2); Najaasat refers to ritual impurities (2).
Name two types of Najaasat as taught in Islamic Religious Education.
Accept the classifications taught in the learner’s course, such as major and minor impurity, with a correct explanation. (1 each)
State the three classes of water in the study of purification.
Pure and purifying water; pure but not purifying water; impure water. (1 each)
Give three circumstances in which Ghusl becomes compulsory.
After sexual intercourse; after ejaculation/wet dream; at the end of menstruation or postnatal bleeding. Any three.
State three occasions when Ghusl is Sunnah.
Before Friday prayer, Eid prayer and entering ihram; accept other recognised Sunnah occasions taught. Any three.
Outline five steps in performing Ghusl.
Make intention; wash hands/private parts; perform Wudhu; pour water over head; wash whole body ensuring water reaches all parts. Any five in correct order.
State three importance of Ghusl.
Restores ritual purity, enables acts of worship requiring major purification, promotes cleanliness. Any three.
State three acts prohibited for a person in Janaba before Ghusl.
Performing Swalah, circumambulating the Kaaba, reciting/touching the Quran according to the taught rulings. Any three.
Define Wudhu.
Ritual washing of specified body parts with clean water in preparation for worship. (2)
State three factors to observe when performing Wudhu.
Use pure water, remove barriers preventing water reaching skin, observe correct order/sequence, make intention. Any three.
Mention three voluntary acts of Wudhu.
Begin with Bismillah, use miswak, wash parts three times, begin with right side, rinse mouth/nose. Any three.
State three things that nullify Wudhu.
Passing urine/faeces/wind, deep sleep or loss of consciousness, other recognised nullifiers taught in class. Any three.
Define Tayammum and state two reasons for performing it.
Dry ritual purification using clean earth/dust (2); lack of water or inability to use water due to illness/danger. (1 each)
State three conditions for valid Tayammum.
Intention; clean earth/dust; water unavailable or its use harmful; perform at appropriate prayer time according to taught rule. Any three.
State three things that nullify Tayammum.
Finding/being able to use water, occurrence of a Wudhu nullifier, end of the reason permitting Tayammum. Any three.
Define Istinjaa and state two materials used for cleansing.
Cleansing private parts after relieving oneself (2); water and suitable clean material such as tissue/stone where permitted. (1 each)
State four toilet etiquettes in Islam.
Enter with left foot, exit with right foot, avoid facing/turning back to Qibla where applicable, maintain privacy, use left hand for cleansing, keep place clean. Any four.
State three situations in which a Muslim may be excused from facing the Qibla.
During genuine danger/fear, when unable due to illness or incapacity, during certain voluntary prayers while travelling on a moving mount/vehicle according to the taught ruling. Any three.
Name the five ordained daily prayers and their usual times.
Fajr—dawn; Dhuhr—after midday; Asr—afternoon; Maghrib—after sunset; Isha—night. (1 each)
State three times when voluntary prayer is prohibited.
At sunrise, when the sun is at its zenith, and at sunset. (1 each)
State four qualities of a Muadhin.
Muslim, mature/sensible, trustworthy, good voice, knowledgeable about prayer times, punctual. Any four.
Give four differences between Adhan and Iqaamah.
Adhan calls people to prayer; Iqaamah announces its immediate start; Adhan is generally longer; Iqaamah is shorter; wording/repetition differs according to taught form. Any four paired contrasts.
Name three types of prayers in Islam.
Fard/obligatory, Sunnah, Nafl/voluntary; other valid categories taught. Any three.

source.basis: Shahada/Tashahhud, Swalah, conditions, Twahara/Najaasat, water classes, Ghusl, Wudhu, Tayammum, Istinjaa, Qibla, prayer times, Muadhin, Adhan/Iqaamah and types of prayer.

subjects.name: Kiswahili
mcq: Ni njia ipi ya jadi ya mawasiliano iliyotajwa kwenye kifungu?
Moshi ni mojawapo ya njia za jadi zilizotajwa.
Simu na mtandao ni njia za kisasa.
Vyombo vya mawasiliano vimeelezwa katika vipengele vingapi?
Kifungu kinataja usafiri, mazungumzo na picha.
Sauti za Kiswahili zimegawanywa katika makundi mawili makuu ya:
Makundi makuu ni irabu na konsonanti.
KI ni konsonanti ikifuatiwa na irabu.
Katika sentensi ‘Mwanafunzi anasoma kitabu’, kitenzi ni:
Isimu jamii huchunguza lugha katika muktadha wa jamii.
structured: Eleza maana ya mawasiliano.
Ni mchakato wa kupeleka au kubadilishana ujumbe kutoka kwa mtu/kitu/mahali hadi kwa mwingine. (2)
Taja njia tatu za jadi za mawasiliano zilizotajwa katika kifungu.
Moshi, ngomezi na kupiga mbiu. (1 kila moja)
Taja njia nne za kisasa za mawasiliano zilizotajwa katika kifungu.
Simu, mtandao, televisheni na wavuti. (1 kila moja)
Taja vipengele vitatu vya vyombo/njia za mawasiliano kulingana na kifungu.
Usafiri, mazungumzo na picha. (1 kila moja)
Eleza maana ya ‘ulimwengu umekuwa kijiji kimoja kikubwa’.
Teknolojia ya mawasiliano imefanya watu wa maeneo mbalimbali kuwasiliana kwa urahisi na haraka kana kwamba wako karibu. (2)
Toa visawe vya maneno haya: (a) waraka (b) televisheni.
(a) barua/hati (1); (b) runinga (1).
Taja aina mbili kuu za sauti za Kiswahili.
Irabu na konsonanti. (1 kila moja)
Taja vigezo vitatu vya kuainisha konsonanti.
Mahali pa kutamkia, namna ya kutamka na hali ya nyuzi sauti/kutumia nyuzi sauti. (1 kila moja)
Taja aina mbili za konsonanti vipasuo.
Kwa mfano /p, b, t, d, k, g/; taja mbili zozote sahihi. (1 kila moja)
Andika majukumu matatu ya lugha.
Mawasiliano, kuelimisha, kuburudisha, kuhifadhi utamaduni, kueleza hisia/kutoa taarifa. Yoyote matatu.
Toa mifano miwili ya maneno yenye muundo wa silabi KI na miwili ya KKI.
KI: baba, kiti, simu (mifano sahihi miwili); KKI: nchi, njia, mbili (mifano sahihi miwili). (1 kila mfano)
Bainisha ngeli za nomino hizi: ngoma, ukuta, macho, ugonjwa, mmea, maiti.

Ngoma—U-ZI (au ngeli ya U-ZI kulingana na matumizi); ukuta—U-ZI; macho—LI-YA; ugonjwa—U-ZI; mmea—U-I; maiti—A-WA/MA-MA kulingana na uainishaji unaotumika. Thibitisha kwa upatanisho sahihi wa sentensi; alama 1 kila moja.
Andika sentensi hizi katika hali ya kukanusha: (a) Mkulima analima shamba. (b) Mwanafunzi anasoma kitabu.
(a) Mkulima halimi shamba. (1); (b) Mwanafunzi hasomi kitabu. (1)
Tambua aina za maneno katika sentensi: Mtoto anacheza vizuri.
Mtoto—nomino (1); anacheza—kitenzi (1); vizuri—kielezi (1).
Toa neno moja lenye kila sauti ambatano: nyw, nd, ngw.
Mifano sahihi ya kila sauti kulingana na matumizi ya Kiswahili sanifu; alama 1 kila moja.
Weka shadda katika maneno: karatasi, shairi, barabara na mto.
Karatási; sháiri; barabára; mtó. (1 kila moja; zingatia silabi yenye mkazo katika matamshi sanifu).
Fafanua maana ya sauti katika lugha.
Ni mlio unaotamkwa na kutumika kujenga maneno katika lugha. (2)
Akifisha: ann musa musa unaitwa musa na nani ann na mama.

structured: Give two examples of metals and three examples of non-metals.
Metals: iron, copper, aluminium, zinc. Any two (2); non-metals: oxygen, carbon, sulphur, nitrogen. Any three (3).
Distinguish between metallic and non-metallic materials.

Metals generally conduct heat/electricity, are lustrous, malleable and ductile; non-metals generally have lower conductivity and may be brittle or non-lustrous. Award valid paired differences up to 4.
Describe six physical properties used to identify materials.
Colour, lustre, hardness, density, texture, strength, malleability, ductility, conductivity, transparency. Any six explained or named (1 each).
State two physical properties of ferrous metals.
Often magnetic; generally strong/hard; may rust/corrode; relatively high density. Any two.
Give two physical properties of non-ferrous metals.
Generally non-magnetic; often corrosion-resistant; may be lightweight; good conductors. Any two.
Distinguish between natural and synthetic non-metallic materials, giving three examples of each.
Natural: obtained from plants/animals/minerals, e.g. cotton, wool, sisal, natural rubber. Synthetic: human-made by chemical/industrial processes, e.g. nylon, PVC, acrylic. Up to 6.

Give five careers involved in processing or using non-metallic materials.

State five factors to consider when selecting a material for an item.
Strength, durability, cost, availability, weight, appearance, safety, ease of working, suitability for purpose. Any five.
Explain the importance of entrepreneurship to Kenya’s economy.
Creates employment, generates income, provides goods/services, promotes innovation, uses local resources, pays taxes and supports economic growth. Any five.
Define personal goals and give two examples.
Targets an individual intends to achieve (2); examples such as improving reading, learning a skill or saving money (any two).
State four benefits of setting personal goals.
Provides direction, motivates effort, helps measure progress, improves time management, builds confidence. Any four.
State five factors to consider when setting personal goals.
Personal interests, abilities, available resources, time, realistic targets, priorities, measurable outcomes. Any five.
Define talent and ability.
Talent is a natural aptitude or special potential; ability is the capacity/skill to perform a task. (1 each)
Give four differences between talent and ability.
Talent is often natural/early evident; ability can be developed through learning; talent may need practice to become skill; ability is demonstrated capacity to perform. Any four clear contrasts.
State five ways learners can nurture talents and abilities.
Practise regularly, seek coaching, participate in clubs/competitions, set goals, accept feedback, use resources, persevere. Any five.
State four ethical issues in using talents and abilities in business.
Honesty, respect for intellectual property, fairness, avoiding exploitation, confidentiality, truthful promotion, giving credit. Any four.
Define business environment.
The internal and external conditions/factors that influence how a business operates. (2)
Distinguish between needs and wants, giving three examples of each.
Needs are essentials for living; wants are desirable but not essential. Examples: food, shelter, clothing; toys, luxury phone, designer accessories. Award 6.
State five characteristics of an entrepreneur.
Creative, innovative, hardworking, confident, willing to take calculated risks, persistent, disciplined, good decision-maker. Any five.
Give five sources of business ideas.
Customer needs, personal skills/hobbies, market research, observation, existing products/services, community problems, new technology. Any five.

Save work; close open applications; use operating system Shut down command; wait until computer powers off before switching off supply. (1 each)
Identify three facilities that ensure proper ventilation in a room.
Windows, doors, ventilators/air vents, fans or air-conditioning. Any three.
